title: SafeFlowMatcher: Safe Planning with Flow Matching
one_liner: To plan fast and safely, generate paths freely first, then correct only the paths you actually use.
lead: A robot needs to plan a path from start to goal while avoiding obstacles. Flow matching is a new way to generate paths very quickly (in just a few steps) by learning the direction the path should flow at each moment. But the fast generated paths can bump into walls or get stuck. SafeFlowMatcher solves this: generate the path freely, then tighten it only where it matters, using formal mathematical guarantees.

problem.h2: Path planners are caught between speed and safety
paras: Most robot planners work by asking a trained neural network to generate the next waypoint step by step, like asking for directions one corner at a time. This is safe (you can check each step) but slow, especially when there are many obstacles.

Flow matching is a new trick: instead of one step at a time, the planner learns which direction to flow at each moment (like a current carrying the plan forward). A robot can follow that flow for many waypoints at once, finishing in just a few steps. The problem: nobody proved the path is actually safe. The network learned its flow from data, not from the obstacle rules, so it might suggest paths that crash into walls or get trapped in corners.

callout.html: Flow matching is very fast (few steps) but offers no safety proof. Safety methods exist but slow down the planner by checking every intermediate guess.

panels.title: 1. The setup
panels.caption: Robot at start corner, goal at far corner, obstacles (walls) block direct paths.

panels.title: 2. Flow matching alone
panels.caption: Network flows freely, finds a shortcut, but path clips corner (unsafe).

panels.title: 3. Check every step (old way)
panels.caption: Every guess checked: safe but slow, costs 100+ steps instead of 4.

panels.title: 4. SafeFlowMatcher: predict then correct
panels.caption: Let flow run free once. Then nudge only the actual executed path away from walls.

panels.caption: Path stays clear of obstacles, still finishes in 4 flow steps, much faster.

steps.text: Run the learned flow matching network once (or a few times) to generate a candidate path from start to goal with no safety checks.
Define a mathematical barrier: a score that is positive far from obstacles and zero or negative at the boundary (touching the wall).
For the actual path the robot will follow, solve a quick optimization (a quadratic program) that nudges waypoints away from barriers while changing the path as little as possible.
Once corrected, mathematically prove that the path obeys the barrier at every point and converges to a safe region in finite time (provably reachable).
Robot follows the corrected path. The proof guarantees no collisions will happen, even in the real world.

paras: The paper changes WHERE safety enforcement happens. Older methods check safety at every intermediate sample during the generation process (before the final path is decided). SafeFlowMatcher instead lets the network generate freely, then refines only the waypoints on the actual executed path.

hidden.h2: The barrier function: measuring distance to danger
hidden.name: Barrier function score
paras: A barrier function is a mathematical score that tells you how close you are to breaking a rule. For obstacles, it is positive when the robot is safely away from walls, zero at the edge of the wall, and negative if the robot is inside the wall (where it should not be). The robot stays safe by keeping this score non-negative.

SafeFlowMatcher computes this score for each waypoint on the executed path and uses it in an optimization that nudges waypoints to keep the score above a safety margin (like keeping a buffer zone around walls).

heat.caption: Darker means closer to obstacles (lower barrier value). Highlighted cells are on the path's boundary.

reads.html: A barrier function is a safety score. When it is positive the robot is safe, when zero or negative the robot is in trouble. SafeFlowMatcher keeps this score positive by nudging waypoints away from obstacles.
Finite-time convergence CBF: a barrier certificate that guarantees the executed path enters and stays in a safe region (distance at least delta away from obstacles) within a bounded number of steps.

mechanism.h2: Why decoupling generation and correction works
paras: Networks learn bad habits when you force them to obey safety rules during generation. If every sample during the learning process must stay away from walls, the network gets confused: it learns to generate paths that hug the walls but never touch them, or it gets stuck in local traps (dead ends). Instead, SafeFlowMatcher lets the network learn from clean data (paths from the training set), so it learns the real structure of good paths. Then, in a separate step, a simple mathematical tool (the barrier function) pushes the final path away from walls. This separation means the network does not unlearn good path patterns, and the correction is purely geometric (push away from shapes), not learned.

The correction is also minimal: instead of recomputing the entire path or reshaping it drastically, the quadratic program nudges waypoints just enough to cross the safety barrier, changing the path as little as possible. This keeps the path smooth and efficient.

stages.s: Network flows once to candidate path
Barrier function scores each waypoint against obstacles
Optimization nudges waypoints to keep barrier positive
Safe, smooth path ready to execute

math.words: penalty = sum of (barrier coefficient times how far waypoint moved squared), plus a penalty for deviating from the original network prediction
math.equation: min sum_k lambda * (b(tau_k))^2 + (tau_k - tau_pred_k)^2 subject to b(tau_k) >= delta for all k
symbols: position of waypoint k (x, y coordinates)
waypoint k from the network prediction before correction
barrier function value at waypoint k (positive = safe)
safety margin (minimum barrier value, e.g., 0.01 units from walls)
weight controlling how much to prioritize barrier violations over path changes

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the network predicts waypoint A at position (5.0, 3.0), and barrier score is -0.05 (inside a wall by 0.05 units). Safety margin delta = 0.01.
Waypoint B at (6.0, 2.5) already has barrier score 0.15 (safe).
Optimization must move A to restore barrier >= 0.01. Nudging A to (5.3, 3.2) raises barrier to +0.02.
Cost of barrier violation before correction: if lambda=10, cost was 10*(-0.05)^2 = 0.025.
Corrected solution trades a small move (0.13) to eliminate a bigger violation penalty, a net savings overall.

math.note: The optimization trades small path changes against staying in the safe zone, ensuring the barrier is respected without distorting the network's good judgment too much.

charts.title: Diffusion-based planner (old way)
charts.note: Works but too slow for real-time robots.

charts.title: SafeFlowMatcher (this paper)
charts.note: 50 times faster because flow matching finishes in 4 steps instead of 100. Same safety proof, cleaner paths because the correction nudges minimally instead of reshaping.

items.b: Network predicts a path that is already safe.
items.html: The correction step does nothing, which is fine. The path is used as-is. No harm.

items.b: The network prediction is so bad that even heavy correction cannot rescue it.
items.html: The optimization might fail to find a correction that respects the barrier, or the corrected path becomes so distorted it no longer reaches the goal. This happens if the network was trained on bad data or if the obstacle field is too dense. Solution: train the network on more diverse hard scenarios.

items.b: The barrier function itself is poorly designed (wrong shape or tuning).
items.html: If the barrier is not tuned to your obstacles (e.g., too tight a margin or wrong obstacle shapes), the path may be over-cautious or even miss the real constraint. The proof only holds if the barrier correctly models the obstacles.

items.b: Done right: barrier tuned, network trained, correction runs fast.
items.html: The path is guaranteed safe by a mathematical proof, not just by luck. The robot can execute it with full confidence.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple 2D maze with start, goal, and walls. Train a flow matching network on paths generated by a slow planner (diffusion or RRT). Then compare three planners: (1) raw flow matching (no safety), (2) an older method that checks safety at every intermediate sample, (3) SafeFlowMatcher. Measure: time per plan (in milliseconds), percentage of test paths that hit walls, and path smoothness (average angle change between steps).
demo.metric_eq: collision_rate = (paths_that_hit_walls / total_paths) * 100; average_time_per_plan = sum_of_times / num_plans; smoothness = average_angle_change_between_consecutive_waypoints
demo.closing: The demo must show SafeFlowMatcher achieving near-zero collisions (the barrier math guarantees safety) while running 10+ times faster than methods that check every intermediate sample (because checking once is faster than checking 100 times). Print the barrier score for each waypoint to verify it stays above the safety margin.
